fixes.explanation: That's the one, baker. David says, “Take up Your shield and buckler; arise and come to my aid.” Notice who he asks to do the moving. He's asking the LORD to get up and come.
You got it, baker. David asks, “may the net they hid ensnare them; may they fall into the hazard they created.” The trap they set for him is the one he asks to have catch them.
Not quite, friend. Hiding isn't the word in this verse. Verse 9 says, “Then my soul will rejoice in the LORD and exult in His salvation.” Rejoicing is what he says comes next.

Right, baker. David's bones say, “Who is like You, O LORD, who delivers the afflicted from the aggressor, the poor and needy from the robber?” He's praising the LORD for delivering the afflicted, the poor and needy. I think David counts himself among them.

Not this time, friend. The shout in verse 10 includes the words “…the poor and needy from the robber?” So David does say the LORD delivers them. His bones are praising the LORD as the One who delivers.
Careful, baker. David says it the other way around. Verse 13 says, “…but my prayers returned unanswered.” He fasted when they were ill, and he says his prayers came back unanswered.

That's right, baker. David says, “But when I stumbled, they assembled in glee; they gathered together against me.” When they were ill, he put on sackcloth, and when he stumbled, they gathered against him. Ouch.

Yes, baker. David says, “Like godless jesters at a feast, they gnashed their teeth at me.” He compares how they acted to godless jesters at a feast, with the teeth grinding. That's a heavy picture, and I think it hurts to read.

Not this time, friend. Verse 16 says, “Like godless jesters at a feast, they gnashed their teeth at me.” Jesters, feast and teeth are all right there in the verse. That's the picture David uses for how they treated him.

That's right, baker. David says, “Then I will give You thanks in the great assembly; I will praise You among many people.” He says he'll give thanks in the great assembly and praise among many people. I think he wants a crowd to hear it.
The cave of Adullam isn't mentioned in this psalm, friend. In verse 18 he says, “Then I will give You thanks in the great assembly…” He's picturing a big crowd, not a cave.
You got it, baker. The enemies say, “Aha, aha! Our eyes have seen!” Then David says, “O LORD, You have seen it; be not silent.” He turns to the LORD and says the LORD has seen it.

That's it, baker. David says, “May those who gloat in my distress be ashamed and confounded; may those who exalt themselves over me be clothed in shame and reproach.” He asks for shame and reproach, not honor. Funny how the ones lifting themselves up get dressed in the opposite.

Not this time, friend. Verse 27 says, “May those who favor my vindication shout for joy and gladness…” So David does want it, and he wants it from the ones on his side. Even in a psalm this heavy, he asks for shouting.

You got it, baker. David wants them to always say, “Exalted be the LORD who delights in His servant’s well-being.” The verse names the servant's well-being as what the LORD delights in. That's a line worth saying always.
Not quite, friend. Verse 28 says nothing about the battle ending. David says, “Then my tongue will proclaim Your righteousness and Your praises all day long.” All day long is the length he gives.
